backchannels.direction: Já and einmitt show listening, often said on an in-breath; jájá said flatly can sound like brushing off.

reactions.direction: Í alvöru? or Nei, er það? for surprise; leiðinlegt að heyra for sympathy; frábært for good news.

cant_hear.direction: Say you hear badly (ég heyri illa í þér) or the line breaks up, then ask them to talk louder.

ask_repeat.direction: Ha? is casual, Fyrirgefðu? politer; ask names letter by letter and echo phone digits.

who_is_calling.direction: Hver er þetta? or Við hvern tala ég? is normal; Icelanders expect the caller to give a name.

examples.text: Þetta er sími hjá {owner}, hver hringir?

wrong_number.direction: Þú hefur valið vitlaust númer, nobody so named lives there; short and friendly.

examples.text: Ég held þú hafir hringt í vitlaust númer.
Hér býr enginn með því nafni.

relay.direction: Ég skila því says {owner} will be told; no promise of a ring-back hour.

sales_decline.direction: Nei takk, ég hef ekki áhuga is direct and normal in Iceland; reasons are not expected.

examples.text: Nei takk, ég hef ekki áhuga.

firm_no.direction: Second push: recall the earlier nei and ask to be taken off the list (bannmerking in Þjóðskrá).

examples.text: Vinsamlegast hringið ekki aftur í þetta númer.

address_forms.direction: First name with þú is normal for almost everyone, including officials; titles are rare.

avoid_service_phrases.direction: Takk fyrir að hringja í þjónustuver and Hvernig get ég aðstoðað? sound like a phone centre.

examples.text: Takk fyrir að hringja í þjónustuverið.
Hvernig get ég aðstoðað þig í dag?

taboo_on_phone.direction: Over-formal þér can sound sarcastic; asking pay or politics of a stranger is out of place.

uncertain: Icelanders mostly use first names and þú even with strangers; formal þér is now rare, so casual vs polite overlap
Backchannels (já, jájá, einmitt, já já) from dictionaries and usage, no call corpus
Inhaled 'já' (ingressive) is common in speech but cannot be shown in text
